title: Claude Code: Nested Sub-Agents, Fallback Chains & Marketplace (2026)
content:
## Overview

The CLI 2026.6 release train brought a cluster of agentic-infrastructure features to Claude Code, aimed at making multi-agent workflows deeper, more resilient, and easier to share. This page covers what shipped and how the pieces fit together.

---

## Nested Sub-Agents

Claude Code now supports **hierarchical agent spawning**: a parent agent can create child agents, and each child can spawn its own children. Reported depth limits vary by build — Claude Code v2.1.172 (June 10, 2026) allowed sub-agents to spawn sub-agents up to 5 levels deep, while the feature is more conservatively documented elsewhere as supporting up to 3 levels. Check `claude --version` behavior against current docs before relying on a specific depth.

This enables **layered task decomposition**: a top-level agent handling a large codebase migration can delegate to module-level agents, which in turn delegate to function-level agents for targeted rewrites — each layer narrowing scope without the coordinator having to track every file itself.

---

## Fallback Model Chains

Rate limits, transient model outages, and cost management all create scenarios where a single target model isn't enough. The new `fallbackModel` configuration lets you specify an **ordered list of models** that Claude Code attempts sequentially:

```json
{
  "model": "claude-sonnet-5",
  "fallbackModel": [
    { "model": "claude-opus-4-8", "maxTokens": 8192, "costCeiling": 5.00 },
    { "model": "claude-haiku-4-5-20251001" }
  ]
}
```

If the primary model returns a rate-limit error or is unavailable, Claude Code automatically tries the next entry in the chain. Each entry supports per-model `maxTokens` and `costCeiling` parameters — `costCeiling` sets a dollar-amount spend cap on that model before Claude Code advances to the next fallback.

---

## Community Tool Marketplace

Claude Code shipped a **registry of community-contributed tools** — linters, formatters, custom slash commands, and specialized refactoring utilities — that can be discovered and installed similarly to package managers in other ecosystems. This lowers the barrier for reusing agentic tooling across teams instead of every project reinventing the same slash commands.

---

## Scoped Permissions & Per-Agent Cost Attribution

**Scoped permissions** let a coordinator restrict what a sub-agent is allowed to do — enforcing least privilege so a subagent handling, say, documentation edits can't also run arbitrary shell commands. Because `permissions.deny` and `permissions.allow` are both security boundaries, any change to either should get the same scrutiny as a security review.

**Per-agent cost attribution** tracks token spend broken down by individual agent/sub-agent, making it possible to see which part of a multi-agent workflow (e.g., a specific reviewer or finder in a fan-out) is driving cost, rather than only seeing an aggregate session total.

---

## MCP Authentication from the Shell

`claude mcp login` authenticates a configured MCP server directly from the shell instead of requiring the interactive `/mcp` menu; `claude mcp logout` clears stored credentials. This is particularly useful in headless/CI contexts where an interactive prompt isn't available.

---

## Shell Mode & Session Improvements

- Shell mode now reacts to command output — e.g., running `npm test` gets an explanation appended automatically rather than requiring a follow-up prompt.
- `/rewind` can resume a conversation from a point **before** `/clear` was run, recovering context that previously would have been discarded.
- Background subagents now surface permission prompts in the **main session** instead of silently auto-denying the action, preventing agents from stalling on a permission they never got a chance to request.

---

## Why It Matters

Taken together, these features push Claude Code further from "one assistant, one context window" toward a small distributed system: nested sub-agents give it recursion, fallback chains give it resilience to individual model failures, scoped permissions and cost attribution give it governance, and the marketplace gives it a way to share reusable building blocks across teams.
